A change of the thing is being made, with the choice of those who bring it being praiseworthy, but weaker and less perfect. For what is being brought is not a full-grown ox, but a calf, lacking in size and strength compared to the perfect ox. Having taken the blood, half is poured into a bowl and half onto the altar. Thus, the life of the one serving is being divided here in a mysterious way. For the blood is taken as a symbol of the soul, whose life is divided equally with us by God, so that we do not live only for ourselves, but also keep the share of the altar. Such is the middle and moderate life, which does not have a harsh and intense drunkenness, nor does it fall into sins due to excessive indulgence. But it has risen to a higher level through caution and is compared to the more perfect ones, although it is lacking in eagerness. With the habit and the quality mentioned being combined into one, a noble and gentle way of life is revealed. For in the relationship between the two, what causes pain in each is eliminated, and the tone of precision is relaxed in the plainness of indulgence. The excess of indulgence is cut off, like a pruning knife cutting off the harshness from the mind, and it will show the straight and blameless way of life. It is good, therefore, to strive for what is better and to pursue virtue more. But as Paul says, each of you has a gift from God.

He, on the one hand, is thus; he, on the other hand, is thus. For being good, the creator of all of us gives opportunities for salvation to the weaker ones. He considers worthy of greater praise the one who strives in the more perfect things. However, he does not deprive of philanthropy the one who does not have much virtue. Just as faces are not like faces, as Solomon says, so the minds of humans are not alike. For the nature of the body is one, and it is perfected through the same parts. But the difference of characters in each person brings about change. Similarly, we will find that the mind, through the same activities, is equal in all, but divided into inequality by the qualities of habits. I think that such a mind is also born through the evangelical parable. For it says, 'The sower went out to sow his seed.' While he was sowing, some fell on the road and on rocky ground, some on thorns, and some on good soil, and it produced fruit, one hundred, one sixty, and one thirty. You see how he said that all the soil was good, but the difference in fruit is irregular. The number one hundred shows those who are perfect in virtue and have reached the highest piety. The number sixty shows those who have made some progress in the things mentioned, and they also have a significant amount of virtue.

The thirty, still inferior, not outside the best land, not deprived of giving fruit, even if they fall short of the perfect and the smallest, are in the third order of those in virtue. For many mansions are with the Father, as the Savior says, determining the measure of honor due to each. The distribution of talents to the servants was like this. To one, five were given; to another, two; to another, one. Although nature is equal to all and has the suitable word for the house, and towards perfection, no difference should be defined in these, but all should be given the five talents equally. Now, the irregularity of the gift brings a certain inequality of conditions, not receiving piety in equal measure. But the one who received the five talents heard: 'Well done, good and faithful servant, you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many, enter into the joy of your lord.' The one who received two talents also receives equal praise and is honored with the same vote. God is not seen as unjust in these things, but rather as good and loving honor. For the kindness towards the one who has fallen short will not diminish the honors for the more perfect, nor will it add what is due to them to the less perfect; but the one who has toiled will receive the reward proportional to their labor, rejoicing, and the grace will fill in what is lacking in the reward.

If someone has the opinion that being envied by others' good deeds is not free, they accuse God's philanthropy without realizing. For it is not the case that the measure of virtue is equally applied to the better ones, and the measure of grace is balanced against the life lived by each, as if by scales. But let us listen to our Savior Christ saying, 'Friend, I am not unjust to you. Did I not agree with you for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. But I want to give to this last one as I gave to you.' Therefore, Paul rouses each person's will to every good work, and warns the inactive mind to shake off laziness, saying, 'Rise, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.' For even if you have fallen asleep as a human, having been overcome by sin like an uncontrolled person, and having been led astray by dark thoughts, now is the time to wake up for salvation and to lift your eyes to the sun of righteousness. The Master, being philanthropic, will receive you, will have mercy on you, and will not turn away from your tears, but will show you to be pure, repentant, and will restore you to piety.

Since it was necessary to follow the obedience of the listeners and the demonstration through signs, he says to him: 'What is in your hand?' And he said: 'A staff.' And he said: 'Throw it on the ground.' And it became a snake; and Moses fled from before it. And the Lord said to Moses: 'Stretch out your hand and seize the tail.' And it became a staff in his hand. But, as I think, through these things the blessed Moses was being taught that those who had been infected with the Egyptian plague, who had greatly gone astray into sin, would be transformed into piety through the honor of the Divine. For a staff sprouts from the earth, but when it turns away from the passions of the flesh and in some way falls from the hand of the lawgiver, then it becomes a venomous snake, bitter towards sin, terrible towards wrath. But when the lawgiver takes it back again, it will be transformed into a good model of the best habit. For we will put the face of the lawgiver on Moses. That God raises up again and changes the one who has slipped into sin due to laziness is, I think, clear to everyone from what has been said. The voices of the prophets will also testify, counseling those who sin to turn back to God from above and below. For our philanthropic Master has not overlooked any opportunity to call all to salvation.

For he was saying: 'Do not fear me, says the Lord, or will you not be cautious before my face? The one who set a boundary for the sea, a perpetual decree, and it will not cross it. But this people had a disobedient and unresponsive heart. They turned away and departed, and did not say in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God.' Sometimes, rebuking more sharply those who were fleeing more shamelessly, he was saying: 'If the Ethiopian changes his skin or the leopard its spots, will you be able to do good, having learned evil things?' For the father of all sin had dominated the race to such an extent that there were very few who honored God and needed to remember the lawgiver they had known.
pass_b_english: As the thing undergoes a transformation, the choice of those who bring it is commendable, yet weaker and less perfect, for what is being brought is not a full-grown ox, but a calf, lacking in size and strength compared to the perfect ox.

The blood is being divided, with half being poured into a bowl and half onto the altar, symbolizing the division of the life of the one serving, which is a mysterious division, with the blood representing the soul, whose life is divided equally with us by God, so that we do not live only for ourselves, but also keep the share of the altar.

This middle and moderate life is one that does not have a harsh and intense character, nor does it fall into sins due to excessive indulgence, but rather, it has risen to a higher level through caution and is compared to the more perfect ones, although it is lacking in eagerness.

As the habit and the quality mentioned are combined into one, a noble and gentle way of life is revealed, one that eliminates what causes pain in each and relaxes the tone of precision in the plainness of indulgence, and the excess of indulgence is cut off, like a pruning knife cutting off the harshness from the mind, and it will show the straight and blameless way of life.

It is good, therefore, to strive for what is better and to pursue virtue more, as Paul says, each of us has a gift from God, and the creator of all things, being good, provides opportunities for salvation to those who are weaker.

He considers worthy of greater praise those who strive for more perfect things, and he does not deprive of his philanthropy those who do not possess much virtue, just as human faces are not identical, so the minds of humans are not alike, and the nature of the body is one, and it is perfected through the same parts, but the difference in characters brings about change in each person.

Similarly, the mind, through the same activities, is equal in all, but it is divided into inequality by the qualities of habits, which is also illustrated by the evangelical parable of the sower, which shows that the soil is good, but the difference in fruit is irregular (Matthew 13:1-23).

The number one hundred represents those who are perfect in virtue and have reached the highest piety, while the number sixty represents those who have made some progress and possess a significant amount of virtue, and the thirty, who are still inferior, are not outside the best land, nor are they deprived of giving fruit, even if they fall short of the perfect and the smallest.

They are in the third order of those in virtue, and their reward is proportional to their labor, for many mansions are with the Father, as the Savior says (John 14:2), determining the measure of honor due to each.

The distribution of talents to the servants is a prime example of this principle, where to one, five talents were given; to another, two; to another, one, although nature is equal to all, and has the suitable word for the house, and towards perfection, no difference should be defined in these, but all should be given the five talents equally.

However, the irregularity of the gift brings a certain inequality of conditions, not receiving piety in equal measure, and the one who received the five talents heard the words of praise and encouragement from the lord, and was set over many, entering into the joy of their lord (Matthew 25:21).

In contrast, the one who received two talents also received equal praise and was honored with the same vote, demonstrating that God is not unjust, but rather good and loving honor, for the kindness towards the one who has fallen short will not diminish the honors for the more perfect, nor will it add what is due to them to the less perfect.

The idea that being envied by others for their good deeds is somehow a restriction on our freedom is a misguided one, for it is not as if the measure of virtue is applied equally to all, with the measure of grace being balanced against the life lived by each individual, as if by scales.

Rather, we should listen to the words of our Savior Christ, who says, 'Friend, I am not unjust to you, did I not agree with you for a denarius? Take what is yours and go, but I want to give to this last one as I gave to you' (Matthew 20:13-15).

This is a call to action, a reminder that we should strive to do good works and not be lazy in our pursuit of virtue, as Paul says, we should rouse our will to every good work and shake off the laziness that can so easily beset us (Ephesians 5:14).

We should rise from our spiritual slumber and lift our eyes to the sun of righteousness, knowing that our Master is a philanthropic one who will receive us with mercy and compassion, even when we have fallen short.

The Lord instructed Moses to throw his staff on the ground, and it became a snake, causing Moses to flee in fear, but when the Lord told Moses to seize the snake by its tail, it transformed back into a staff.
This miraculous event taught Moses that those who had been infected with the Egyptian plague and had strayed into sin could be transformed into piety through the honor of the Divine.

Just as a staff can sprout from the earth, but becomes a venomous snake when it turns away from the passions of the flesh, so too can humans become bitter towards sin and terrible towards wrath when they fall away from the lawgiver's guidance.
Nevertheless, when the lawgiver takes them back, they can be transformed into a good model of the best habit, and their face can be restored to its original state.
The voices of the prophets also testify to this, counseling those who sin to turn back to God from above and below, and it is not a matter of contention for us.
The Lord says, 'Do not fear me, or will you not be cautious before my face? The one who set a boundary for the sea, a perpetual decree, and it will not cross it' (Jeremiah 5:22).
However, this people had a disobedient and unresponsive heart, and they turned away, departing without saying in their heart, 'Let us fear the Lord our God' (Jeremiah 5:24).
Sometimes, the Lord rebuked them more sharply, saying, 'If the Ethiopian changes his skin or the leopard its spots, will you be able to do good, having learned evil things?' (Jeremiah 13:23).
The father of all sin had dominated the race to such an extent that there were very few who honored God and needed to remember the lawgiver they had known.

The Lord's words are a call to repentance, and we should heed them, for our Master is a philanthropic one who will receive us with mercy and compassion, even when we have fallen short, and it is not a matter of contention for us, for it is clear to everyone that God raises up again and changes the one who has slipped into sin due to laziness.

As Paul says, we should rouse our will to every good work, and shake off the laziness that can so easily beset us, and rise from our spiritual slumber, and lift our eyes to the sun of righteousness, and Christ will shine on us, for even if we have fallen asleep as humans, having been overcome by sin, now is the time to wake up for salvation, and the Master, being philanthropic, will receive us, will have mercy on us, and will not turn away from our tears, but will show us to be pure, repentant, and will restore us to piety.
